w: Behind the reading room shelves sits the J.S. Battye Library, the working archive of Western Australian history - diaries, maps and photographs of a state still being pieced together. The State Library's real job is preservation: digitising a heritage that would otherwise fade with the paper it's printed on.
s: WA's paper memory, digitised page by page
_facts: research, education, reference and public lending library in the Perth Cultural Centre
portfolio agency of the WA Department of Local Government, Sport and Cultural Industries
particular responsibility for collecting, preserving and digitising WA's heritage materials
J.S. Battye Library of West Australian History is its dedicated historical section

w: One museum, six outposts scattered clear across Western Australia - shipwrecks in Fremantle, gold-rush relics in Kalgoorlie, regional history in Albany and Geraldton. The Perth flagship, Boola Bardip, anchors a statutory network set up in 1969 to keep a state twice the size of most countries honest about its own past.
s: One museum's name, six WA outposts
_facts: statutory authority under the Museum Act 1969, six main sites
state museum WA Museum Boola Bardip is in the Perth Cultural Centre
other sites: WA Maritime Museum and WA Shipwrecks Museum in Fremantle, Museum of the Great Southern in Albany, Museum of Geraldton, Museum of the Goldfields in Kalgoorlie-Boulder

w: Known to the Noongar as Mudurup, Cottesloe has drawn swimmers since the railway reached its sheltered, reef-broken waters. The neotraditional Indiana Tea House has watched the sand since 1996, while every year the beach turns gallery for Sculpture by the Sea and starting line for the Rottnest Channel Swim.
s: Perth's reef-sheltered icon of a beach
_facts: known in Noongar language as Mudurup, one of WA's most iconic locations
popularity from proximity to Perth, train access, shelter from summer breezes, offshore reefs
heritage-listed since 2005; current beachfront structure the Indiana Tea House built 1996 in neotraditional style
hosts the Rottnest Channel Swim and Sculpture by the Sea; around 600,000 visitors a year

w: Built in fits and starts across a century and a half, St Mary's wears its unfinished decades openly: the Great Depression halted a 1920s Gothic makeover partway, leaving a mismatched nave for seventy years. A 2006-2009 rebuild finally gave it a second spire and finished what the 1930s couldn't afford.
s: A cathedral finished seventy years late
_facts: officially the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Perth
first phase completed 1865; 1920s plans for a larger Perpendicular Gothic replacement interrupted by the Great Depression
closed for construction 2006, reopened December 2009 with a second spire and underground parish centre

w: Alan Bond built his corporate monument on the site of a fight to save the old Palace Hotel - campaigners lost, and the tycoon's fifty-storey tower rose in its place, briefly Perth's tallest. It served as Bond Corporation's headquarters until his empire collapsed, then passed to Bankwest, then a mining company.
s: Alan Bond's tower, built where a hotel lost its fight
_facts: fifty-storey office building, 1981-1988, 214m to roof, Perth's tallest until 1992
site previously the Palace Hotel; organised opposition to its demolition failed
Alan Bond acquired the site; building served as HQ of Bond's companies until their collapse, later Bankwest until 2012, then South32 from 2015

w: Perth's public art collection lives partly behind a courthouse facade: the Centenary Galleries occupy the old court building, linked to the main gallery that opened alongside it in 1979. Justice and art, side by side in the Cultural Centre.
s: The gallery wing that used to be a courthouse
_facts: public art gallery, part of Perth Cultural Centre, managed by a WA government department
current main building opened 1979
linked to the old court house, now the Centenary Galleries

w: More than a million people walk through Karrakatta's cypress-lined entrance every year - the Waiting House, designed by colonial architect George Temple-Poole, still greets them as it has since 1899. A wheelwright named Robert Creighton got the first grave; WA's first mausoleum followed almost a century later.
_facts: opened for burials 1899, first burial wheelwright Robert Creighton
attracts more than one million visitors a year; cypress trees near main entrance a hallmark
crematorium onsite; WA's first mausoleum opened 1995; entrance 'Waiting House' designed by George Temple-Poole

w: The very first permanent structure the Swan River colonists put up, in 1831 - and it was a gaol, not a home or a church. Only the stone fort on West Wallabi Island beat it into the ground. Fremantle's oldest surviving European building still crowns Arthur Head, once better known as Gaol Hill.
s: WA's oldest building - and it was a prison
_facts: first permanent building in the Swan River Colony, built late 1830, opened 1831
second oldest surviving European building in WA after the Wiebbe Hayes Stone Fort on West Wallabi Island
located at Arthur Head, Fremantle; the location also referred to as Gaol Hill

w: When it opened in 1904, His Majesty's was the biggest theatre in the country and, so the record suggests, Perth's first building poured in reinforced concrete. It's since been declared a State Heritage Icon and is believed the last working Edwardian theatre standing in Australia, still home to WA Ballet and Opera.
_facts: Edwardian Baroque theatre built 1902-1904, largest theatre in Australia at opening, seating over 2,500
thought to be the first reinforced concrete building in Perth
State Heritage Icon, believed the only remaining working Edwardian theatre in Australia, home to WA Ballet and WA Opera

w: Bushland now covers the hill where Western Australia first talked to the world by radio - the old Applecross Wireless Station's buildings survive intact as the Wireless Hill Museum, ringed by 40 hectares of protected scrub that doubles as one of Perth's better urban walks.
s: Where WA's early wireless station still stands
_facts: 40-hectare park in Ardross, site of the former Applecross Wireless Station, an early WA radio station
station buildings preserved, house the Wireless Hill Museum
listed on the Register of the National Estate and State Register of Heritage Places; significant urban bushland

w: This Oberon-class submarine fired the first armed Mark 48 torpedo the Royal Australian Navy ever launched, sinking the decommissioned Colac as a target. Retired herself in 1995 after 26 years in service, she now sits preserved at the Maritime Museum, hull open for anyone curious about life inside a Cold War sub.
s: The sub that fired the RAN's first armed torpedo
_facts: Oberon-class submarine, entered RAN service 1969, one of six Oberons built by Scotts Shipbuilding
first RAN submarine to deploy with the ANZUK force and to fire an armed Mark 48 torpedo, sinking target ship Colac
decommissioned 1995, preserved as a museum ship at the WA Maritime Museum

w: Nothing showy marks Perth's oldest mosque, just the quiet distinction of being the second purpose-built mosque raised anywhere in Australia - a modest brick marker of how long Muslim communities have called this city home.
_facts: the oldest mosque in Perth
the second oldest purpose-built mosque in Australia

w: Climb Reabold Hill inside Bold Park and you get both halves of Perth in one turn - the city skyline one way, the Indian Ocean the other, barely a kilometre off. At 437 hectares of protected bushland minutes from the beach suburbs, it's a rare urban reserve big enough to actually get lost in.
s: 437 hectares, city on one side, ocean the other
_facts: 437-hectare urban bushland around Reabold Hill in City Beach, 8km west of Perth CBD
western border less than 1km from the Indian Ocean; Perry Lakes reserve adjacent to the east
hilly topography allows views of both the city and the ocean
